title: Political Parties
subject: civics
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Political Science: 20 marks). There is no map item from this chapter. The list of national parties is updated to the Election Commission's 2023 recognition; the NCERT book prints an older list.

sections.title: Why do we need political parties?

blocks.title: An election without parties
blocks.body:
Imagine a Lok Sabha election with 543 seats and no parties. Every candidate is independent. After the result, who becomes Prime Minister? Who promises to bring in a new policy for farmers or students, and who is responsible if it fails?

Parties solve this problem. They bring people with similar views together, put forward policies, form governments and act as the opposition. This chapter asks what parties do, how many we need, which parties India has, and what is wrong with them today.

blocks.title: Building a party for the voiceless
blocks.body:
**Kanshi Ram** left a government job in Pune to organise dalit, adivasi and backward class employees. In **1984** he founded the **Bahujan Samaj Party**, which aimed to win political power for the 'bahujan samaj', the majority of people who had been kept away from power.

Within a decade, the BSP became one of the main parties of Uttar Pradesh. His work shows how a political party can give a voice to people who were left out of decision making.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in politics, public policy, election management, journalism, political research and law.

blocks.question: What would most likely happen in a large democracy without political parties?
options: No one could promise major policy changes, and no one would be responsible for running the country
Elections would become more peaceful and simple
The government would be stronger and more responsible
blocks.explanation: Representative democracy cannot work without political parties.

sections.title: Meaning and functions of political parties

blocks.title: What parties are, what they do and why we need them
blocks.body:
**Meaning:** a **political party** is a group of people who come together to **contest elections and hold power** in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promote the **collective good**. Since there can be different views on what is good for all, parties try to persuade people why their policies are better than others. They seek to implement these policies by winning popular support through elections.
- Parties reflect fundamental political divisions in a society. A party is known by which **part** of society it stands for, which policies it supports and whose interests it upholds.
- **Partisanship:** a party is about a part of society, and thus involves partisanship: an inclination to take a side and an inability to take a balanced view.
- **Three components of a party:** the **leaders**, the **active members** and the **followers**.

**Functions of political parties:**
1. **Contest elections:** in most democracies, elections are fought mainly among candidates put up by political parties. In some countries such as the **USA**, members and supporters of a party choose its candidates; in **India**, top party leaders choose candidates.
2. **Put forward policies and programmes:** parties put forward different policies and programmes, and voters choose from them. Parties reduce a vast number of opinions into a few basic positions that they support. A government is expected to base its policies on the line taken by the ruling party.
3. **Make laws:** laws are debated and passed in the legislature. Since most members of the legislature belong to a party, they go by the direction of the party leadership, irrespective of their personal opinions.
4. **Form and run governments:** parties recruit leaders, train them and then make them ministers to run the government in the way they want. The big policy decisions are taken by the political executive, which comes from the parties.
5. **Play the role of opposition:** parties that lose elections play the role of opposition to the parties in power, by voicing different views and criticising the government for its failures or wrong policies. Opposition parties also mobilise opposition to the government.
6. **Shape public opinion:** parties raise and highlight issues. They have lakhs of members and activists spread all over the country. Many of the pressure groups are extensions of political parties among different sections of society. Parties sometimes also launch movements for the resolution of problems faced by people.
7. **Provide access to government machinery and welfare schemes:** for an ordinary citizen, it is easier to approach a local party leader than a government officer. Parties have to be responsive to people's needs and demands; otherwise people can reject them in the next election.

**Necessity of political parties:** we need parties because they perform all these functions. Imagine a situation without parties:
- Every candidate in the elections would be **independent**. No one would be able to make any promises to the people about major policy changes.
- The government may be formed, but its utility would remain uncertain. Elected representatives would be accountable to their constituency for what they do in the locality, but **no one would be responsible for how the country is run**.
- We can see this in the **non-party based elections to panchayats** in many states: although parties do not contest formally, the village often splits into factions, each putting up a 'panel' of candidates.
- The rise of political parties is directly linked to the emergence of **representative democracies**. As societies became large and complex, they needed some agency to gather different views on various issues and present these to the government. That is why almost all countries of the world have political parties.

blocks.question: What are the three components of a political party?
options: candidates, the Election Commission and the press
blocks.explanation: A party has leaders, active members and followers.
option_feedback: The Election Commission is not part of a party.

blocks.question: In India, who chooses the candidates of a party for elections?
options: all members and supporters of the party
blocks.explanation: In the USA, members and supporters choose candidates; in India, top leaders do.
option_feedback: The President has no such role.

sections.title: How many parties should we have?

blocks.title: Party systems and alliances
blocks.body:
In a democracy, any group of citizens is free to form a political party. In India, more than **750 parties** are registered with the Election Commission. But not all of these are serious contenders in elections. So the question is not how many parties exist, but how many are effective.

**One-party system:** in some countries, only one party is allowed to control and run the government. In **China**, only the **Communist Party** is allowed to rule. Although, legally speaking, people are free to form political parties, the electoral system does not permit free competition for power. A one-party system is **not a good option** because it is not a democratic option: any democratic system must allow at least two parties to compete in elections and provide a fair chance for the competing parties to come to power.

**Two-party system:** in some countries, power usually changes between two main parties. Several other parties may exist, contest elections and win a few seats, but only the two main parties have a serious chance of winning a majority and forming the government. The **United States of America** and the **United Kingdom** are examples.

**Multi-party system:** when several parties compete for power, and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power either on their own strength or in alliance with others. **India** has a multi-party system.
- **Alliance or front:** when several parties in a multi-party system join hands for the purpose of contesting elections and winning power. In India, there were three major alliances in the **2004** parliamentary elections: the **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)**, the **United Progressive Alliance (UPA)** and the **Left Front**.
- A multi-party system often appears very messy and can lead to political instability, but it allows a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation.

**Which system is best?** There is no simple answer. A party system is not something a country can choose. It evolves over a long time, depending on the **nature of society**, its **social and regional divisions**, its **history of politics** and its **system of elections**. Each country develops a party system conditioned by its special circumstances. India evolved a multi-party system because its social and geographical diversity is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties.

blocks.title: Party systems compared
blocks.body:
| Party system | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **One-party system** | only one party is allowed to control and run the government; voters have no real choice, so it is not a democratic option | China (Communist Party) |
| **Two-party system** | power usually changes between two main parties; others exist but rarely win more than a few seats | USA, United Kingdom |
| **Multi-party system** | several parties compete, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power, alone or in alliance | India |

blocks.question: Why is a one-party system not a good option?
options: It allows too many parties to win seats
It is not a democratic option, as voters have no real choice
It leads to too many coalitions
blocks.explanation: Democracy needs at least two parties competing fairly for power.
option_feedback: That is not the main reason.

blocks.question: Why does India have a multi-party system?
options: Its social and geographical diversity is not easily absorbed by two or three parties
The Constitution allows only many parties
Two-party systems are illegal in India
blocks.explanation: A party system evolves with a country's society, divisions, history and elections.
option_feedback: The Constitution does not fix the number.
A party system evolves; it is not chosen.

blocks.title: Recognised parties in India
blocks.body:
Democracies that follow a federal system all over the world tend to have two kinds of parties: parties present in only one of the federal units, and parties present in several or all units of the federation. India is no exception.

**Recognition by the Election Commission:** every party in the country has to **register** with the Election Commission. While the Commission treats all parties equally, it offers some special facilities to large and established parties. These parties are given a **unique symbol**: only the official candidates of that party can use that election symbol. Parties that get this privilege and some other special facilities are **'recognised'** by the Election Commission.
- **State party:** a party that secures at least **six per cent** of the total votes in an election to the **Legislative Assembly** of a state and wins at least **two seats**.
- **National party:** a party that secures at least **six per cent** of the total votes in **Lok Sabha** elections or Assembly elections in **four states**, and wins at least **four seats** in the Lok Sabha.

**National parties (as recognised by the Election Commission since 2023):** the NCERT book lists the parties recognised when it was printed; the Commission's list in 2023 had **six** national parties:
- **Indian National Congress (INC):** founded in **1885**; it has split many times. It played a dominant role in Indian politics for several decades after independence. A **centrist** party in its ideological orientation, it espouses **secularism** and the **welfare of weaker sections and minorities**. It led the **United Progressive Alliance (UPA)** government from **2004 to 2014**.
- **Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP):** founded in **1980** by reviving the **Bharatiya Jana Sangh**, formed by **Syama Prasad Mukherjee** in **1951**. It wants to build a strong and modern India by drawing inspiration from India's ancient culture and values; **cultural nationalism (Hindutva)** is an important element of its conception of Indian nationhood, and Deendayal Upadhyaya's ideas of **'integral humanism'** guide it. It leads the **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)** and formed the government at the Centre after the **2014, 2019 and 2024** elections.
- **Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP):** formed in **1984** under the leadership of **Kanshi Ram**. It seeks to represent and secure power for the **bahujan samaj**, which includes the **dalits, adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities**. It draws inspiration from the ideas and teachings of **Sahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Periyar Ramaswami Naicker and Babasaheb Ambedkar**. Its main base is in **Uttar Pradesh**.
- **Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI-M):** founded in **1964**. It believes in **Marxism-Leninism**, supports **socialism, secularism and democracy**, and opposes **imperialism and communalism**. It enjoys strong support in **West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura**.
- **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP):** founded in **2012**; recognised as a national party in **2023**.
- **National People's Party (NPP):** founded in **2013** by **P.A. Sangma**; recognised as a national party in **2019**, the first party from the **North-East** to get this status.

**State parties:** other than these, most of the major parties are classified as **'state parties'**, commonly called regional parties. Some of them are all-India parties that happen to have succeeded only in some states. Parties like the **Biju Janata Dal, Sikkim Democratic Front, Mizo National Front** and **Telugu Desam Party** are conscious about their state identity.
- Over the last three decades, the number and strength of these parties has expanded. This made the **Parliament of India more diverse** politically.
- No one national party was able to secure a majority in the Lok Sabha on its own from **1989 until 2014**. As a result, national parties were compelled to form alliances with state parties. Since 1996, nearly every one of the state parties has got an opportunity to be part of one or the other **national-level coalition government**. This has contributed to the **strengthening of federalism and democracy** in our country.

blocks.title: National parties of India
blocks.body:
| National party | Founded | Key ideas |
|---|---|---|
| **Indian National Congress (INC)** | 1885 | centrist; secularism and welfare of weaker sections and minorities; led the UPA (2004–2014) |
| **Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)** | 1980 (from the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, 1951) | cultural nationalism; 'integral humanism'; leads the NDA; formed the government in 2014, 2019 and 2024 |
| **Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP)** | 1984 (Kanshi Ram) | power for the bahujan samaj: dalits, adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities; inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar and Ambedkar; main base in Uttar Pradesh |
| **Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI-M)** | 1964 | Marxism-Leninism; socialism, secularism and democracy; opposes imperialism and communalism; strong in Kerala, West Bengal and Tripura |
| **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)** | 2012 | national party since 2023; anti-corruption and governance issues |
| **National People's Party (NPP)** | 2013 (P.A. Sangma) | national party since 2019; first party from the North-East with national status; based in Meghalaya |

blocks.question: To be recognised as a state party, a party must win at least:
options: 6% of the votes in a state Assembly election and 2 seats
6% of the votes in Lok Sabha elections and 4 Lok Sabha seats
50% of the votes in the state
blocks.explanation: Recognised parties get a unique election symbol.
option_feedback: It needs 6% of votes and 2 seats.
That is part of the condition for a national party.

blocks.question: Which party was founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984?
blocks.explanation: The BSP represents the bahujan samaj.
option_feedback: It was founded by P.A. Sangma in 2013.

sections.title: Challenges to political parties and reforms

blocks.title: What is wrong with parties, and how can they be reformed?
blocks.body:
Since parties are the most visible face of democracy, people blame parties for whatever is wrong with the working of democracy. Popular dissatisfaction and criticism has focused on **four problem areas**:

1. **Lack of internal democracy:** all over the world, there is a tendency for parties to concentrate power in **one or a few leaders** at the top. Parties do not keep **membership registers**, do not hold **organisational meetings**, and do not conduct **internal elections** regularly. Ordinary members do not get sufficient information about what happens inside the party, and do not have the means or connections needed to influence decisions. Leaders assume greater power to make decisions in the name of the party. Those who disagree with the leadership find it difficult to continue in the party. More than loyalty to party principles and policies, **personal loyalty to the leader** becomes more important.
2. **Dynastic succession:** since most parties do not practise open and transparent procedures, there are very few ways for an ordinary worker to rise to the top. Those who happen to be the leaders are in a position of unfair advantage to favour people close to them or even their family members. In many parties, the **top positions are always controlled by members of one family**. This is unfair to other members and bad for democracy, since people who do not have adequate experience or popular support come to occupy positions of power. This tendency is present in some measure all over the world, including in some older democracies.
3. **Money and muscle power:** since parties are focused only on winning elections, they tend to use short-cuts. They nominate candidates who have or can raise **lots of money**. Rich people and companies who give funds to parties tend to influence their policies and decisions. In some cases, parties support **criminals** who can win elections. Democrats all over the world are worried about the increasing role of rich people and big companies in democratic politics.
4. **Lack of meaningful choice:** in order to offer meaningful choice, parties must be significantly different. In recent years, there has been a decline in the **ideological differences** among parties in most parts of the world. In our country too, the differences among major parties on economic issues have reduced. Those who want really different policies have no option available to them. Sometimes people cannot even elect very different leaders, because the same set of leaders keep shifting from one party to another.

**Steps already taken to reform parties:**
- **Anti-defection law:** **defection** means changing party allegiance from the party on which a person got elected to a different party. Many MLAs and MPs were indulging in defection to become ministers or for cash rewards. The Constitution was amended (**52nd Amendment, 1985**) so that if an MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will **lose the seat** in the legislature. This has helped bring defection down, but it has made dissent even more difficult: MPs and MLAs have to accept whatever the party leaders decide.
- **Affidavit:** the **Supreme Court** passed an order (**2003**) to reduce the influence of money and criminals. Now it is mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to file an **affidavit** giving details of their **property and criminal cases** pending against them. This information is made public. But there is no system of check on whether the information is true.
- **Election Commission order:** the Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to hold their **organisational elections** and file their **income tax returns**. Parties have started doing so, but sometimes it is a mere formality.

**Suggestions for further reform:**
- A **law to regulate the internal affairs** of political parties: to maintain a register of members, follow their own constitution, have an independent authority to act as a judge in case of party disputes, and hold open elections to the highest posts.
- Make it mandatory for parties to give a minimum number of tickets, about **one-third, to women** candidates; similarly, there should be a quota for women in the decision-making bodies of the party.
- **State funding of elections:** the government should give parties money to support their election expenses, in kind (petrol, paper, telephone and so on) or in cash, on the basis of votes secured in the last election.

Legal reforms need care: over-regulation can be counter-productive, and parties may find ways to cheat the law. Two other ways are important: **people can put pressure** on parties through petitions, publicity and agitations, and through the media and movements; and **people who want reform can join parties** themselves, since the quality of democracy depends on the degree of public participation.

blocks.question: A law that makes an MP or MLA lose the seat for changing parties is the:
blocks.explanation: The Constitution was amended in 1985 to stop defection.
option_feedback: The affidavit is about property and criminal cases.
That is a suggested reform about election expenses.
That is an Election Commission order for internal elections.

blocks.question: Which is a challenge to political parties in India?
blocks.explanation: Top positions are often controlled by members of one family.
option_feedback: The problem is a decline in ideological differences.
The problem is lack of transparency.
The problem is too few internal elections.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Functions: "CPL-FOSA"**: Contest elections, Policies, Laws, Form government, Opposition, Shape opinion, Access to schemes.
- **Components: "LAF"**: Leaders, Active members, Followers.
- **Party systems: China = 1, USA/UK = 2, India = many.**
- **Recognition: "6% + 2 seats" (state); "6% in Lok Sabha or 4 states + 4 Lok Sabha seats" (national).**
- **National parties and years: "INC 1885, CPI-M 1964, BJP 1980, BSP 1984, AAP 2012, NPP 2013".**
- **Challenges: "I-D-M-C"**: Internal democracy, Dynastic succession, Money and muscle, Choice.
- **Reforms already taken: "Defection 1985, Affidavit 2003, Elections and tax returns (EC)".**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying China has no parties: it has a **one-party** system (Communist Party).
2. Saying India has a two-party system: India has a **multi-party** system.
3. Saying the Election Commission decides which party system India has: party systems **evolve** with society, divisions, history and elections.
4. Mixing up the recognition rules: a **state** party needs 6% of Assembly votes and **2 seats**; a **national** party needs 6% in Lok Sabha or 4 states and **4 Lok Sabha seats**.
5. Saying the anti-defection law increased dissent: it reduced defection but made **dissent more difficult**.
6. Writing that the affidavit order came from Parliament: it came from the **Supreme Court**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Collect the election symbols of the national parties and two state parties of your state. Ask groups to find out the party's founding year, its main ideas and whether it is national or state, and present a one-minute 'party profile'.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: If you joined a political party, which one challenge from this chapter would you most want to fix first, and how?

blocks.body:
- **Chapter 1 (Power-sharing):** sharing power among parties and coalitions.
- **Chapter 2 (Federalism):** regional parties and coalition governments after 1990.
- **Chapter 5 (Outcomes of Democracy):** accountable and responsive government.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Lack of internal democracy and dynastic succession are major challenges to political parties.' Explain in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Political parties tend to concentrate power in one or a few leaders at the top. They do not keep membership registers, hold organisational meetings or conduct regular internal elections, so ordinary members have little information or influence, and those who disagree find it hard to stay. Personal loyalty to the leader becomes more important than loyalty to party principles. Because parties lack open and transparent procedures, there are very few ways for an ordinary worker to rise to the top. Leaders favour people close to them or their family members, and in many parties the top posts are always held by one family. This is unfair to other members and bad for democracy, as people without adequate experience or popular support come to occupy positions of power.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power; it has leaders, active members and followers.
- Parties contest elections, put forward policies, make laws, form governments, act as opposition, shape opinion and give access to government schemes.
- Party systems: one-party (China), two-party (USA, UK), multi-party (India); party systems evolve, they are not chosen.
- The Election Commission recognises state and national parties (6% votes plus seats) and gives them unique symbols.
- Challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, lack of meaningful choice.
- Reforms: anti-defection law, affidavits on property and criminal cases, organisational elections and tax returns; suggestions include regulating internal affairs, tickets for women and state funding.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper had a 5-mark question with a choice: explain the significant role of parties in democracy (functions), or analyse how leadership succession is a challenge to parties in India (dynastic succession).
- 3/5-mark favourites: functions, necessity of parties, party systems, national party profiles, challenges and reforms.
- In 5-mark answers, write five separate points with a heading for each.

blocks.back: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government, agreeing on policies to promote the collective good.
Changing party allegiance from the party on which a person got elected to a different party.

blocks.front: What is an alliance or front?
blocks.back: When several parties in a multi-party system join hands to contest elections and win power, such as the NDA and UPA.

blocks.front: Name the four challenges to political parties.
blocks.back: Lack of internal democracy; dynastic succession; growing role of money and muscle power; lack of meaningful choice.
